Content:
The standard inner product of [MATH: \Bbb R^n,] i.e. the dot product, does not meet the criteria of an inner product on [MATH: \Bbb C^n.]

Content:
For example, if [MATH: \langle \,\cdot\,, \,\cdot\, \rangle] is a valid inner product on [MATH: \Bbb C^n,] then for any vector [MATH: \mathbf a \in \Bbb C^n,] we must have

Content:
[MATH: \langle\mathbf a, \, \mathbf a\rangle \ge 0.]

Content:
But for many vectors in [MATH: \Bbb C^n,] such as [MATH: [\textrm{i}; 0]] in [MATH: \Bbb C^2,] the dot product fails to satisfy this criterion:

Content:
[MATH: [\textrm{i}; 0] ⋅ [\textrm{i}; 0]|= \textrm{i}^{2} + 0^{2}; = − 1; < 0×]

Content:
Thankfully, there is an elegant way to generalize the dot product to satisfy the desired criterion on [MATH: \Bbb C^n.] We can just take the complex conjugate of each element in the right vector before carrying out the dot product.

Content:
More formally, for two vectors [MATH: \mathbf x, \mathbf y\in \mathbb C^n] given by

Content:
[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; ⋮; x_{n}]]

Content:
we define the standard Hermitian inner product as

Content:
[MATH: ⟨x, y⟩|= x_{1} ⋅ y_{1}^(―) + x_{2} ⋅ y_{2}^(―) + ⋯ + x_{n} ⋅ y_{n}^(―); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} ⋅ y_{i}^(―),]

Content:
where [MATH: \overline{y_i}] is the complex conjugate of [MATH: y_i.]

Content:
Using the standard Hermitian inner product instead of the dot product, our desired criterion is satisfied:

Content:
[MATH: ⟨[\textrm{i}; 0], [\textrm{i}; 0]⟩|= \textrm{i} ⋅ \textrm{i}^(―) + 0 ⋅ 0^(―); = \textrm{i} ⋅ (− \textrm{i}) + 0 ⋅ 0; = 1 + 0; = 1; ≥ 0✓]

Content:
It can be verified that the Hermitian inner product satisfies all the criteria of an inner product on [MATH: \Bbb C^n.]

Content:
Furthermore, since the complex conjugate leaves real numbers unchanged, the Hermitian inner product simplifies to the dot product on [MATH: \Bbb R^n.] In other words, the dot product is just a special case of the Hermitian inner product!

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over [MATH: \mathbb{C}] satisfies the following properties:

  • It is linear in the first argument. For any [MATH: \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n] and any [MATH: \alpha \in \mathbb{C},] we have

    [MATH: \qquad] [MATH: \langle \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad] and [MATH: \quad \langle \alpha \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \alpha \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.]

  • It is antilinear in the second argument. For any [MATH: \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n] and any [MATH: \alpha \in \mathbb{C},] we have

    [MATH: \qquad] [MATH: \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad] and [MATH: \quad \langle \mathbf{a}, \alpha\mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\alpha} \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.]

  • It has conjugate symmetry. For any [MATH: \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n,] we have

    [MATH: \qquad] [MATH: \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle}.]

  • It is positive-definite. For any [MATH: \mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{C}^n,] we have

    [MATH: \qquad] [MATH: \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle] is a non-negative real number, and [MATH: \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = 0] if and only if [MATH: \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}.]

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is false. The inner product over [MATH: \mathbb{C}] is a complex number in general.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, by the linearity in the first argument and the antilinearity in the second argument, we have [MATH: \langle \mathrm{i}\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \mathrm{i}\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \overline{\, \mathrm{i}\, } \mathbf{b} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a},- \mathrm{i} \mathbf{b} \rangle] for any [MATH: \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n.]

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, by the linearity in the first argument and the antilinearity in the second argument, we have [MATH: \langle\mathrm{i} \mathbf{a},\mathrm{i} \mathbf{a} \rangle =\mathrm{i}\cdot \bar{ \mathrm{i} }\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = -\mathrm{i}^2\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle= \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle] for any [MATH: \mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{C}^n.] But by positive-definiteness, this is a nonnegative real number.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The standard inner product of [MATH: \Bbb R^n,] i.e. the dot product, does not meet the criteria of an inner product on [MATH: \Bbb C^n.]

Content:
For example, if [MATH: \langle \,\cdot\,, \,\cdot\, \rangle] is a valid inner product on [MATH: \Bbb C^n,] then for any vector [MATH: \mathbf a \in \Bbb C^n,] we must have

Content:
[MATH: \langle\mathbf a, \, \mathbf a\rangle \ge 0.]

Content:
But for many vectors in [MATH: \Bbb C^n,] such as [MATH: [\textrm{i}; 0]] in [MATH: \Bbb C^2,] the dot product fails to satisfy this criterion:

Content:
[MATH: [\textrm{i}; 0] ⋅ [\textrm{i}; 0]|= \textrm{i}^{2} + 0^{2}; = − 1; < 0×]

Content:
Thankfully, there is an elegant way to generalize the dot product to satisfy the desired criterion on [MATH: \Bbb C^n.] We can just take the complex conjugate of each element in the right vector before carrying out the dot product.

Content:
More formally, for two vectors [MATH: \mathbf x, \mathbf y\in \mathbb C^n] given by

Content:
[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; ⋮; x_{n}]]

Content:
we define the standard Hermitian inner product as

Content:
[MATH: ⟨x, y⟩|= x_{1} ⋅ y_{1}^(―) + x_{2} ⋅ y_{2}^(―) + ⋯ + x_{n} ⋅ y_{n}^(―); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} ⋅ y_{i}^(―),]

Content:
where [MATH: \overline{y_i}] is the complex conjugate of [MATH: y_i.]

Content:
Using the standard Hermitian inner product instead of the dot product, our desired criterion is satisfied:

Content:
[MATH: ⟨[\textrm{i}; 0], [\textrm{i}; 0]⟩|= \textrm{i} ⋅ \textrm{i}^(―) + 0 ⋅ 0^(―); = \textrm{i} ⋅ (− \textrm{i}) + 0 ⋅ 0; = 1 + 0; = 1; ≥ 0✓]

Content:
It can be verified that the Hermitian inner product satisfies all the criteria of an inner product on [MATH: \Bbb C^n.]

Content:
Furthermore, since the complex conjugate leaves real numbers unchanged, the Hermitian inner product simplifies to the dot product on [MATH: \Bbb R^n.] In other words, the dot product is just a special case of the Hermitian inner product!
